- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

3	Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.

13	Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
14	Both improve extraction quality \emph{and} produce evidence annotations.
15	However, encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy, and their evidence mechanisms (binary sentence classification) do not transfer to generative architectures.
16	The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.
17	
18	This gap reflects a deeper structural difference between evidence in encoder and generative frameworks.

20	The evidence signal \emph{regularizes} the encoder and improves extraction.
21	In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
22	Evidence production in this setting is not an auxiliary signal but an additional generation burden that competes with the extraction objective for model capacity.
23	The fundamental asymmetry is clear: encoder evidence helps extraction; generative evidence costs extraction capacity.
24	This distinction motivates a systematic investigation of how to produce faithful evidence within LLM-based DocRE without sacrificing the extraction gains that make these models attractive.
25	
26	We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task for LLMs and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training optimization paradigms: online reinforcement learning via GRPO \citep{shao2024deepseekmath}, offline preference optimization via DPO \citep{rafailov2023direct}, and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR \citep{zelikman2022star}).
27	Our experiments across 85+ configurations, spanning four model scales (1.7B to 8B), two model families, and two datasets, reveal three principal findings.
28	\textbf{First}, we identify a \emph{decoupling spectrum}: the strength of RL optimization pressure correlates with the severity of evidence-extraction decoupling.

\section{Introduction}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
Recent LLM-based approaches have closed this gap: \citet{wan2024genres} recast DocRE as constrained generation, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy.
Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
Relation extraction outputs are consumed downstream by knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows.
When a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.
Without machine-generated evidence, this verification requires exhaustive manual review of the input document for every predicted relation.
Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
Both improve extraction quality \emph{and} produce evidence annotations.
However, encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy, and their evidence mechanisms (binary sentence classification) do not transfer to generative architectures.
The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a deeper structural difference between evidence in encoder and generative frameworks.
In SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision.
The evidence signal \emph{regularizes} the encoder and improves extraction.
In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
Evidence production in this setting is not an auxiliary signal but an additional generation burden that competes with the extraction objective for model capacity.
The fundamental asymmetry is clear: encoder evidence helps extraction; generative evidence costs extraction capacity.
This distinction motivates a systematic investigation of how to produce faithful evidence within LLM-based DocRE without sacrificing the extraction gains that make these models attractive.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task for LLMs and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training optimization paradigms: online reinforcement learning via GRPO \citep{shao2024deepseekmath}, offline preference optimization via DPO \citep{rafailov2023direct}, and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR \citep{zelikman2022star}).
Our experiments across 85+ configurations, spanning four model scales (1.7B to 8B), two model families, and two datasets, reveal three principal findings.
\textbf{First}, we identify a \emph{decoupling spectrum}: the strength of RL optimization pressure correlates with the severity of evidence-extraction decoupling.
GRPO with QLoRA \citep{hu2022lora} produces catastrophic decoupling where extraction accuracy collapses to near zero; GRPO with full-precision training shows mild decoupling; DPO exhibits gradual degradation; and RSFT maintains stable joint performance.
QLoRA acts as a catastrophic amplifier of the underlying optimization conflict rather than its root cause.
\textbf{Second}, we discover a \emph{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of jointly producing evidence and relations follows a non-monotonic pattern across model scales.
At 1.7B parameters, evidence supervision provides an implicit regularization benefit of +8 percentage points (pp) in Rel-F1; at 4B, it imposes a $-$7.5pp penalty; at 8B, the tax approaches zero.
This non-linear pattern overturns the naive assumption that evidence generation uniformly harms extraction.
\textbf{Third}, RSFT with NLI-based Claim-Evidence Decomposition (CED) scoring emerges as the only effective optimization route.
By selecting high-quality training samples through output filtering rather than applying gradient-based optimization pressure, RSFT sidesteps the multi-objective competition that destabilizes RL and preference methods.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We formalize \textbf{evidence-grounded document-level relation extraction} as a generation task for LLMs, defining structured output formats that jointly produce relation triplets and their supporting evidence sentences.

    \item We characterize a \textbf{decoupling spectrum} across optimization paradigms: RL optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none). We introduce the EDCR diagnostic metric, which captures this relationship with method-level $\rho = -0.965$.

    \item We identify a \textbf{scale-dependent evidence tax}: a non-monotonic cost pattern across 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters that overturns the assumption that evidence production uniformly degrades extraction quality.

    \item We establish \textbf{RSFT with NLI-based CED scoring} as an effective solution, achieving +4.92pp Ign-F1 over SFT at 4B scale. Our 1.7B RSFT model (50.50 Ign-F1) matches 8B SFT performance (50.51), enabling deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction at reduced computational cost.

    \item We present a \textbf{comprehensive empirical study} spanning 85+ experiments across four model scales, two model families, two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), and three optimization paradigms, providing the first systematic analysis of evidence production in generative DocRE.
\end{enumerate}

## Core Insight

**统一主线 (D131)**: Evidence generation in LLM-based DocRE is not a fixed cost — its role depends on **model capacity** (scale-dependent tax), **training paradigm** (decoupling spectrum), and **data quality** (NLI-based filtering). RSFT navigates this landscape by eliminating the tax while preserving evidence faithfulness.

本文提出 **evidence-grounded DocRE** 作为新任务范式：LLM 同时输出关系三元组和支撑证据句。核心发现是 evidence generation 的效果并非简单的有益/有害二分，而是一个由三个维度决定的 landscape：

1. **Model capacity × evidence tax** (C3): 1.7B 从 evidence 获益（tax=-6.2pp，隐式正则化），4B 付出代价（tax=+7.5pp），8B/14B 趋零。这不是噪声——跨 4 个 Qwen scale + LLaMA 跨家族验证一致。
2. **Training paradigm × decoupling** (C2): RL 优化压力与 evidence-extraction decoupling severity 正相关（GRPO catastrophic > DPO gradual > RSFT none）。越激进的优化越破坏 RE-evidence 平衡。
3. **Data quality × training reliability** (C1+C3): NLI-based quality filtering (CED/flat-NLI) 不仅提升 mean performance（+3-5pp），更 dramatically 压缩 seed variance（7-31×）。1.7B RSFT（std=0.09pp）比 8B SFT（std=3.72pp）更 predictable——小模型通过 quality filtering 获得大模型才有的稳定性。

**RSFT 是唯一同时在三个维度上表现良好的方法**：不引入 decoupling（维度2），压缩 evidence tax 至接近零（维度1），且通过 quality filtering 保证 training reliability（维度3）。

CED (Contrastive Evidence Discrimination) 是一种 NLI-based 候选筛选函数，与 flat-NLI 统计不可区分（D078 p=0.44），但均显著优于 random/no scoring。CED 因可解释性优势作为默认推荐。

## Story Arc (D131: unified narrative)

**One-sentence pitch**: Evidence generation in DocRE is a landscape shaped by capacity, paradigm, and data quality — and RSFT is the only method that navigates all three axes successfully.

1. **Problem**: LLM DocRE 无证据 → 部署障碍
2. **New task**: evidence-grounded DocRE — 同时生成关系和证据
3. **The landscape** (统一主线的三个 facet):
   - **3a. Capacity axis** (C3): evidence tax 是 scale-dependent 的——1.7B 获益（-6.2pp），4B 付代价（+7.5pp），8B/14B 趋零。推翻"evidence 总有代价"
   - **3b. Paradigm axis** (C2): RL optimization pressure 与 decoupling severity 正相关（GRPO catastrophic > DPO gradual > RSFT none）。QLoRA 放大 mild→catastrophic（intra-task trade-off，非 inter-task forgetting）
   - **3c. Quality axis** (C1): NLI-based scoring 不仅提升 mean（+3-5pp），更压缩 variance 7-31×。Training reliability 是 quality filtering 的本质效应
4. **RSFT navigates the landscape**: 唯一同时在三个轴上表现良好的方法——无 decoupling + 压缩 tax + 保证 reliability
5. **Practical toolkit**: CED reranker（response-level，恢复 97% evidence 代价），joint generation > post-hoc retrieval（EDCR 低 11pp）
6. **Diagnostic**: EDCR 双层诊断——方法级量化 decoupling，per-relation 级定位薄弱关系类型
7. **Scaling evidence**: 4 Qwen scales (1.7B/4B/8B/14B) + LLaMA-8B 跨家族 + Re-DocRED 跨数据集
8. **Mechanistic decomposition**: duplication regularization (主因, monotonic decline) + truncation asymmetry + capacity residual — 解释 WHY 而非只报 WHAT

### Claim 5 (NEW — Scaling): Evidence Tax 呈 Non-Monotonic Scaling Pattern（D079/D082/D083）
- **核心发现**: evidence generation 的代价不是固定的——它与模型容量呈非线性关系
  - **1.7B (Qwen3-1.7B)**: tax=-6.2pp (evidence beneficial) — evidence generation 起隐式正则化作用，防止小模型过拟合（D083 公平子集分析确认）
  - **4B (Qwen3-4B)**: tax=+7.5pp (cost, D076: evi 39.74% / no-evi 47.21%) — 标准 evidence generation 负担，模型容量不足以同时优化两个目标
  - **8B Qwen (Qwen3-8B)**: tax≈0 — 模型容量足够 absorb evidence generation 的额外负担
  - **8B LLaMA (LLaMA-3.1-8B)**: tax=+0.7pp — 跨家族确认，8B 规模 evidence tax 趋近于零（微弱代价）
- **Non-monotonic 解释**: 小模型从 evidence 的正则化效应获益 > 生成负担；中等模型容量不足以同时做好两件事；大模型容量充裕，两个目标互不干扰
- **Mechanistic analysis (plan_020 完成)**：3 层机制解释 scale-dependent tax：
  - **(1) Duplication regularization（主因）**: monotonic decline — 1.7B 27.5pp gap (60.5%→33.0%), 4B 12.1pp gap (43.2%→31.1%), 8B 3.7pp gap (32.9%→29.2%)。正则化效应随容量增大递减
  - **(2) Truncation asymmetry**: 1.7B Δ=19pp (no-evi worse), 4B Δ=2pp (neutral), 8B Δ=-9pp (evi worse, tokens 消耗输出预算)
  - **(3) Fair comparison residual**: 排除截断后（442/985 docs），1.7B evidence 仍提升 6.2pp (ign_f1)，8B Qwen -0.3pp，8B LLaMA +0.3pp — 证明 1.7B 有真实 reasoning scaffold 效应
  - **4B "capacity valley" 确认**: duplication 已低(31.1%，接近 8B 29.2%)不需正则化，truncation 中性(29.2% vs 31.2%)，但容量不足同时做 RE + evidence generation → 纯开销(tax=+7.5pp, D076 protocol)
- **论文叙事**: "Evidence as implicit regularization" — 推翻 "evidence 总有代价" 的简单叙事。60.5%→33.0% duplication rate 是最有冲击力的数据点。建议 4 张图（duplication rate / truncation crossover / fair comparison / doc complexity）
- **Cross-family robustness (D130 审计)**: LLaMA-8B RSFT 3-seed mean=0.5654 (std=0.52pp, s42=0.5714/s43=0.5662/s44=0.5587), Δ=+2.70pp over SFT (0.5654 vs 0.5384)。std=0.52pp ≈ Qwen3-8B 0.50pp——variance compression 跨架构一致（待 SFT 3-seed 完成后计算压缩倍数）
- **Evidence 角色转化 (D130, ⚠️ 待方法论对齐)**: SFT tax=+0.68pp 来自两个独立训练模型对比（training-time effect），RSFT tax=-1.52pp 来自同一模型不同推理（inference-time effect）。Reviewer 指出不可直接对比。需补充：LLaMA SFT s42 adapter + no_evidence 推理的标准化 eval，才能得到 inference-time SFT tax。标准化 eval 已安排
- **RSFT 弥合 scale gap (D094→D102→D118)**: 1.7B RSFT 3-seed mean=**0.5119** (std=0.09pp) vs 8B SFT 3-seed mean=**0.5019** (std=3.72pp)，Δ=+1.0pp, p=0.69 不显著——CED-RSFT 使 1.7B 模型**接近** 4.7× 大的 8B SFT，但差异在统计噪声内。"surpasses" claim 被 D118 否定（8B SFT s43=0.5324 拉高均值），回退为 "approaches"

- **14B SFT evidence tax ≈ 0 (D117)**: 14B with-evidence=0.5507, no-evidence=0.5510, tax=+0.03pp——14B 容量完全 absorb evidence 生成负担，延续 8B 的 neutral 趋势

- **D112 Method B (full pipeline from s44 SFT)**: 4B RSFT bf16 ign_f1=**0.5152** (+4.18pp over SFT s44=0.4734)——确认 RSFT 不依赖特定 SFT seed，pipeline 可复现

### Deep Error Analysis (plan_021 完成)
- **SFT→RSFT 三大改善机制（3 尺度一致）**:
  - **(1) Truncation FN 减少 -16~22%**: 1.7B 获益最大 (-841 FN)。与 evidence tax 的 truncation asymmetry 互洽
  - **(2) Hallucinated FP 减少 -6~12%**: LLaMA 获益最大 (-593, -11.8%)。CED filtering 淘汰了低质量 hallucinated responses
  - **(3) Duplicate 减少 -11~20%**: 1.7B 获益最大 (-20.2%)。与 duplication regularization 发现完全对应
- **未改善**: Evidence exact match 变化 <0.4pp（evidence grounding 需专门信号）; Relation confusion FP 稳定; Rare relation FN 稳定
- **与 Evidence Tax 分析的闭环**: Evidence regularization (tax analysis) ↔ RSFT format regularization (error analysis) 是同一机制的两个视角。小模型需要结构化约束来避免退化输出
- **Per-relation 获益最大**: participant, conflict, league, screenwriter, operator, contains_admin_territory — 跨句推理或长尾实体关系
- **Over-citation trend**: 大模型 over-citation 增加 (12%→17%)，边际预测的 evidence 精度下降
- **k=1 vs k=3 对比**: 1.7B + LLaMA k=1 优于 k=3; 8B k=3 略优 (+0.57 ign_f1)
- **关键 negative finding**: Evidence quality 完全不变 (exact match Δ<0.4pp) → RSFT 改善 RE 但不改善 evidence grounding → 需要专门的 evidence-aware 训练信号 → 直接 motivates GRPO+CED。形成完整 pipeline 故事线：SFT→RSFT(RE提升)→GRPO+CED(evidence提升)
- **Limitation**: "FN: other" 增加 ~13-15%（RSFT 消除 easy errors 但不解决 hard cases: 复杂推理、知识缺失）

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns (updated from Dream, D068-D083)

### RC1: "Online RL" 标题过度声称（Dream 三档一致 Critical）

- **D068/D069 修正**: 重新定位为 "RL optimization pressure correlates with decoupling severity"——不是 GRPO 特有问题，而是 RL-for-IE 的通用梯度

### RC2: GRPO G=4 太小 + LoRA confound（Dream 三档一致 Major）

### RC3: CED 不显著优于 flat-NLI（Dream 三档一致 Major）

- **应对**: 不再声称 CED > flat-NLI；论文定位为 "NLI-based scoring 是关键（CED 和 flat-NLI 均有效），CED 因可解释性作为默认推荐"

### RC4: RSFT 不新颖
- 不声称 RSFT 是贡献；贡献在于任务定义 + decoupling 发现 + EDCR
- 诚实定位 RSFT 为 STaR (NeurIPS 2022) 单轮变体 + domain-specific quality filter

### RC12: SAIS 说 evidence 有用，为何 FREIGE 说 evidence 有害？（文献审查 2026-05-16）
- **关键区分**: discriminative evidence *retrieval*（SAIS/DREEAM — 分类句子是否为证据，作为监督信号提升 RE）vs generative evidence *production*（FREIGE — LLM 生成完整证据文本，额外生成负担导致 scale-dependent 代价）
- SAIS 的 evidence supervision 是分类任务，不增加输出长度；FREIGE 的 evidence generation 显著增加生成序列长度，模型需分配容量同时完成 RE + evidence 生成
- **D079/D083 新弹药**: evidence tax 是 scale-dependent 的——1.7B 模型中 evidence 有益（tax=-6.2pp），与 SAIS 的发现方向一致。这说明 evidence 的效果取决于模型容量和任务范式的交互，而非简单的有害/有益二分
- **应对**: Related Work 中精准讨论此对比，明确 FREIGE 研究的是 *generative production* 设定下的代价，与 *retrieval* 设定下的增益不矛盾——两者揭示了 evidence 在不同范式下的不同角色

### RC13: 单模型单数据集泛化性不足（D077 scope 扩展）
- ~~plan_006: Qwen3-1.7B / 8B model size ablation~~ ✅ D079/D083 完成
- ~~plan_016: LLaMA-3.1-8B cross-family validation~~ ✅ D082 完成
- ~~plan_007: Re-DocRED cross-dataset evaluation~~ ✅ D080 完成

- **DREEAM 协议确认**: DREEAM 的 evi_f1=54.01% 等价于我们的 evi_f1_joint（FP/FN triples 计入分母）

- 观察项，等 test set 数据

- BM25 entity_only k=2: evi_f1_joint=0.347, EDCR=0.766 → 弱于 RSFT joint generation (0.361, EDCR=0.654)

- NLI retrieval 变体降为 rebuttal 备用

### RC11: "RL 不遗忘" 文献与 Claim 2 的张力（文献扫描 2026-05-16）
- 近期多篇论文（arXiv 2507.05386, 2506.23508, 2509.04259）论证 RL fine-tuning 天然缓解 catastrophic forgetting
- **关键区分**: FREIGE 的 decoupling 是 **intra-task multi-objective trade-off**（RE 抽取 vs evidence 生成两个优化目标的竞争），不是 **inter-task forgetting**（丢失预训练知识）。两者机制不同

- **应对**: Related Work / Discussion 中显式回应这组文献，区分 intra-task trade-off vs inter-task forgetting

### CRITICAL 发现

1. **[severity: critical] 贡献数量不匹配 (line 38-48)**: Intro 列出 **5 条 contributions**，但 D103 明确将 4→3 贡献重构（C1: evidence-grounded DocRE + RSFT/NLI, C2: decoupling spectrum, C3: scale-dependent tax + variance compression），D131 进一步统一为"landscape 的三个 facet"。5 条列表完全违背重构决策。

2. **[severity: critical] 过时数字 "+8pp" (line 32)**: 写 "implicit regularization benefit of +8 percentage points (pp) in Rel-F1"。paper_framing.md 关键 claim 调整明确记录: `"+8pp" → fair subset "+6.2pp"，Abstract 加 "on a controlled evaluation subset"`。当前 intro 仍用旧数据。

3. **[severity: critical] "matches 8B SFT" 未回退 (line 45)**: 写 "Our 1.7B RSFT model (50.50 Ign-F1) matches 8B SFT performance (50.51)"。D118 已否定 "surpasses/matches" claim，回退为 "approaches"。且具体数字错误: ROADMAP 显示 1.7B RSFT=51.19, 8B SFT=50.19，非 50.50/50.51。

4. **[severity: critical] 因果语言未修正 (line 30)**: "QLoRA acts as a catastrophic amplifier" — D068/D069 修正所有因果 claim → 观察性描述，paper_framing.md 明确写 `"acts as catastrophic amplifier" → "co-occurs with"`。

5. **[severity: critical] "non-monotonic" 应为 "scale-dependent" (line 31-33)**: paper_framing.md 关键调整: `"scale-dependent" 替代 "non-monotonic"（4 个数据点支撑趋势，非严格 non-monotonic claim）`。

### WARNING 发现

6. **[severity: warning] "+4.92pp Ign-F1 over SFT at 4B" (line 45)**: 此数字在 paper_framing.md 中找不到对应。最接近的: RSFT CED s43(best)=+6.11pp, CED mean=+5.20pp。+4.92pp 来源不明，可能是过时版本。

2	
3	Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
4	Recent approaches based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition for end-to-end extraction, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
5	These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy.
6	Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
7	In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.
8	
9	The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
10	Relation extraction outputs feed downstream knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows; when a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.
11	Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
12	Both produce evidence annotations and improve extraction quality, but encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy.
13	The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.
14	
15	This gap reflects a deeper structural difference in how evidence functions across architectures and scales.
16	In encoder-based methods such as SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision; the evidence signal regularizes the encoder and improves extraction at minimal cost.
17	In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
18	Yet the role of this generation cost is not fixed.
19	It depends on at least three factors: \emph{model capacity}, where small models benefit from the implicit regularization that evidence provides while mid-scale models suffer from capacity competition and larger models absorb the overhead; \emph{optimization paradigm}, where gradient-based methods create destructive trade-offs between evidence and extraction objectives while discrete sample selection avoids them entirely; and \emph{training data quality}, where filtering based on Natural Language Inference (NLI) scores can transform evidence from an optimization burden into a learning scaffold.
20	Understanding this landscape is a prerequisite for deploying evidence-grounded extraction systems that are both accurate and verifiable.
21	
22	We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training paradigms: online reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}), offline preference optimization via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; \citealt{rafailov2023direct}), and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star}).

These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy.
Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
Relation extraction outputs feed downstream knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows; when a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.

This gap reflects a deeper structural difference in how evidence functions across architectures and scales.
In encoder-based methods such as SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision; the evidence signal regularizes the encoder and improves extraction at minimal cost.

\begin{abstract}

Large Language Model (LLM) based Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) now matches or exceeds encoder baselines in extraction accuracy, yet these methods output bare relation triplets without identifying which sentences support each prediction.
Deployment contexts such as clinical knowledge bases and legal due-diligence systems require verifiable evidence that users can trace to source text.
Encoder-based evidence methods (SAIS, DREEAM) provide supporting sentences but trail LLM approaches in accuracy, so the community faces a gap between extraction performance and output verifiability.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and systematically compare three post-training paradigms: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT) across 85+ configurations spanning three fully evaluated scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B SFT validation, two model families, and two datasets.
We use the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR) as a diagnostic tool and Natural Language Inference (NLI) based scoring for sample selection.

Our experiments reveal that evidence generation plays a scale-dependent role shaped by three interacting factors.
Along the capacity dimension, the evidence tax varies from beneficial ($-$6.2pp Ign-F1 on a controlled subset at 1.7B) to costly (+7.5pp at 4B) to negligible at $\geq$8B (positive $=$ cost).
Along the paradigm dimension, optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic, DPO gradual, RSFT none).
Along the data quality dimension, RSFT with NLI-based scoring navigates this landscape through output filtering rather than gradient-based pressure.

RSFT improves mean Ign-F1 across tested scales (+1.2 to +6.6pp) with 7--31$\times$ variance compression.
Our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) performance (50.19, std 3.72pp) while being 4.7$\times$ smaller and substantially more predictable.

\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}
2	
3	Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
4	Recent approaches based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition for end-to-end extraction, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
5	These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy.
6	Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
7	In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.
8	
9	The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
10	Relation extraction outputs feed downstream knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows; when a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.
11	Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
12	Both produce evidence annotations and improve extraction quality, but encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy.
13	The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.
14	
15	This gap reflects a deeper structural difference in how evidence functions across architectures and scales.
16	In encoder-based methods such as SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision; the evidence signal regularizes the encoder and improves extraction at minimal cost.
17	In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
18	Yet the role of this generation cost is not fixed.
19	It depends on at least three factors: \emph{model capacity}, where small models benefit from the implicit regularization that evidence provides while mid-scale models suffer from capacity competition and larger models absorb the overhead; \emph{optimization paradigm}, where gradient-based methods create destructive trade-offs between evidence and extraction objectives while discrete sample selection avoids them entirely; and \emph{training data quality}, where filtering based on Natural Language Inference (NLI) scores can transform evidence from an optimization burden into a learning scaffold.
20	Understanding this landscape is a prerequisite for deploying evidence-grounded extraction systems that are both accurate and verifiable.
21	
22	We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training paradigms: online reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}), offline preference optimization via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; \citealt{rafailov2023direct}), and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star}).
23	Our experiments span three model scales with full RSFT evaluation (1.7B, 4B, 8B), 14B SFT validation, two model families, and two datasets across 85+ configurations. They reveal that the role of evidence generation is governed by three interacting factors.
24	Along the \emph{capacity dimension}, the evidence tax is scale-dependent: evidence generation provides implicit regularization at 1.7B ($-$6.2pp Ign-F1 on a controlled evaluation subset), imposes a substantial cost at 4B (+7.5pp), and approaches zero at $\geq$8B parameters.
25	Along the \emph{paradigm dimension}, we observe a decoupling spectrum in which the strength of optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none); catastrophic extraction collapse co-occurs with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA; \citealt{hu2022lora}) in GRPO, though full-precision GRPO maintains extraction above the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baseline with only mild decoupling (EDCR 0.6318 vs.\ SFT 0.6797), which indicates that the collapse is not inherent to online RL when sufficient precision is available.
26	Along the \emph{data quality dimension}, RSFT with NLI-based scoring navigates this landscape by selecting high-quality training samples through output filtering rather than applying gradient-based pressure; it improves mean Ign-F1 across tested scales (+1.2 to +6.6pp) while compressing training variance 7--31$\times$.
27	
28	Our contributions are as follows:
29	\begin{enumerate}
30	    \item We map the \textbf{evidence generation landscape} through a comprehensive empirical study spanning 85+ experiments across three fully evaluated model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B SFT validation, two model families, two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), and three optimization paradigms. We identify a \textbf{scale-dependent evidence tax} that varies from beneficial ($-$6.2pp at 1.7B) to costly (+7.5pp at 4B) to negligible ($\geq$8B). This pattern challenges the assumption that evidence generation uniformly harms extraction.
31	
32	    \item We characterize a \textbf{decoupling spectrum} that explains why gradient-based paradigms fail at joint evidence-and-extraction generation: RL optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none). We introduce the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR) as a diagnostic metric, validated through per-relation analysis ($\rho = -0.79$, $n = 76$, $p < 0.001$).
33	
34	    \item We establish \textbf{RSFT with NLI-based scoring} as an effective navigation strategy for this landscape. RSFT improves mean Ign-F1 across tested scales (+1.2 to +6.6pp) with 7--31$\times$ variance compression, and our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B SFT performance (50.19, std 3.72pp) while being 4.7$\times$ smaller and substantially more predictable. This combination enables deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction.
35	\end{enumerate}
36

The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a deeper structural difference in how evidence functions across architectures and scales.
In encoder-based methods such as SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision; the evidence signal regularizes the encoder and improves extraction at minimal cost.
In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
Yet the role of this generation cost is not fixed.
It depends on at least three factors: \emph{model capacity}, where small models benefit from the implicit regularization that evidence provides while mid-scale models suffer from capacity competition and larger models absorb the overhead; \emph{optimization paradigm}, where gradient-based methods create destructive trade-offs between evidence and extraction objectives while discrete sample selection avoids them entirely; and \emph{training data quality}, where filtering based on Natural Language Inference (NLI) scores can transform evidence from an optimization burden into a learning scaffold.
Understanding this landscape is a prerequisite for deploying evidence-grounded extraction systems that are both accurate and verifiable.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training paradigms: online reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}), offline preference optimization via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; \citealt{rafailov2023direct}), and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star}).
Our experiments span three model scales with full RSFT evaluation (1.7B, 4B, 8B), 14B SFT validation, two model families, and two datasets across 85+ configurations. They reveal that the role of evidence generation is governed by three interacting factors.
Along the \emph{capacity dimension}, the evidence tax is scale-dependent: evidence generation provides implicit regularization at 1.7B ($-$6.2pp Ign-F1 on a controlled evaluation subset), imposes a substantial cost at 4B (+7.5pp), and approaches zero at $\geq$8B parameters.
Along the \emph{paradigm dimension}, we observe a decoupling spectrum in which the strength of optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none); catastrophic extraction collapse co-occurs with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA; \citealt{hu2022lora}) in GRPO, though full-precision GRPO maintains extraction above the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baseline with only mild decoupling (EDCR 0.6318 vs.\ SFT 0.6797), which indicates that the collapse is not inherent to online RL when sufficient precision is available.
Along the \emph{data quality dimension}, RSFT with NLI-based scoring navigates this landscape by selecting high-quality training samples through output filtering rather than applying gradient-based pressure; it improves mean Ign-F1 across tested scales (+1.2 to +6.6pp) while compressing training variance 7--31$\times$.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We map the \textbf{evidence generation landscape} through a comprehensive empirical study spanning 85+ experiments across three fully evaluated model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B SFT validation, two model families, two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), and three optimization paradigms. We identify a \textbf{scale-dependent evidence tax} that varies from beneficial ($-$6.2pp at 1.7B) to costly (+7.5pp at 4B) to negligible ($\geq$8B). This pattern challenges the assumption that evidence generation uniformly harms extraction.

    \item We characterize a \textbf{decoupling spectrum} that explains why gradient-based paradigms fail at joint evidence-and-extraction generation: RL optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none). We introduce the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR) as a diagnostic metric, validated through per-relation analysis ($\rho = -0.79$, $n = 76$, $p < 0.001$).

    \item We establish \textbf{RSFT with NLI-based scoring} as an effective navigation strategy for this landscape. RSFT improves mean Ign-F1 across tested scales (+1.2 to +6.6pp) with 7--31$\times$ variance compression, and our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B SFT performance (50.19, std 3.72pp) while being 4.7$\times$ smaller and substantially more predictable. This combination enables deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires reasoning across sentence boundaries to identify relations between entity pairs.
DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} established the first large-scale benchmark for this task, catalyzing a line of encoder-based methods that treat DocRE as classification over entity pair representations.
ATLOP \citep{zhou2021atlop} introduced adaptive thresholding for multi-label prediction and localized context pooling for entity representations.
A parallel thread incorporates sentence-level evidence into these architectures.
SAIS \citep{xiao2022sais} introduced evidence supervision as an auxiliary training signal and showed that joint evidence prediction improves extraction through data augmentation and ensemble inference.
DREEAM \citep{ma2023dreeam} extended this approach with dynamic memory-based evidence retrieval that guides attention to supporting sentences.
EIDER \citep{xie2022eider} jointly trains an evidence extractor and fuses evidence representations into the relation classifier.
In all three systems, evidence identification is binary sentence classification over a fixed candidate set, a formulation that adds no output complexity.
Recent work has recast DocRE for large language models.
AutoRE \citep{autore2024} fine-tunes LLMs with QLoRA using a relation-head-facts decomposition; \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame extraction as multi-choice reading comprehension; RelPrior \citep{wang2025relprior} uses relation priors to guide LLM-based extraction; GLiDRE \citep{zhang2025glidre} presents a generalist lightweight approach; Ru-LLM \citep{wang2025rullm} incorporates logical rule constraints; and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods match or surpass encoder baselines but produce bare triplets without evidence.
The critical distinction lies in computational nature: in SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is classification that regularizes the encoder without increasing output length; in LLM-based DocRE, evidence requires additional output tokens per triple, imposing costs that depend on model capacity and optimization strategy.
Whether this cost is inevitable or can be mitigated is the central question of our work.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}) eliminates the separate value network by computing advantages within groups.
Subsequent work addresses failure modes: DAPO \citep{yu2025dapo} prevents entropy collapse, Dr.\ GRPO \citep{liu2025drgrpo} corrects length bias, and multi-objective variants \citep{liu2026gdpo,ito2025mogrpo} handle competing reward signals.
Applications to structured IE include R1-RE \citep{dai2025r1re} and REAR \citep{wang2025rear}.
Direct Preference Optimization \citep{rafailov2023direct} reformulates RLHF as implicit reward maximization.
Our decoupling spectrum addresses a distinct phenomenon from catastrophic forgetting \citep{jin2025rl_panacea}: extraction and evidence compete within a single task, compounded by QLoRA's constrained parameter space \citep{gao2023scaling,moskovitz2024constrained}.

Our setting connects to multi-task learning, where evidence and extraction constitute competing objectives.
The decoupling we observe under GRPO resembles negative transfer \citep{ruder2017overview,standley2020tasks,yu2020gradient}: extraction and evidence compete for gradient capacity, amplified by constrained settings (QLoRA).
RSFT avoids this by operating on discrete outputs rather than gradients, extending the sample-and-select principle \citep{wang2023selfconsistency} to structured IE with joint quality scoring.

Evidence faithfulness evaluation has received increasing attention: \citet{li2025drift} propose dual-reward inference for faithful rationale generation, and \citet{zhang2024infuse} introduce fine-grained NLI-based faithfulness metrics for summarization.
Our CED scoring builds on similar NLI-based principles but targets evidence-relation entailment rather than free-form rationales.

\citet{zelikman2022star} introduced STaR for iterative self-improvement; \citet{dong2023raft} generalize this with reward-model-based sample filtering; recent analysis shows rejection sampling implicitly performs PPO-like optimization \citep{tang2025rsftppo}.
Our RSFT is a single-round variant applied to evidence-grounded DocRE with CED/NLI scoring as a domain-specific quality filter.
Because RSFT selects complete outputs rather than differentiating through a reward signal, it cannot exploit the extraction-evidence trade-off that gradient methods discover, inherently preserving joint quality.

40	\label{sec:ablation_full}
41	
42	Table~\ref{tab:ablation_full} reports the complete RSFT ablation across scoring functions, top-$k$ values, and random seeds. RSFT CED $k{=}1$ achieves a four-seed mean Ign-F1 of 44.66 (standard deviation 0.49), confirming robust improvement over the SFT s42 baseline (39.74). The three-seed mean reported in Table~\ref{tab:main} (44.82, seeds 42/43/44) is slightly higher because it excludes the lowest seed (s45: 44.16). Random selection RSFT $k{=}1$ (41.14 Ign-F1), which samples from the same candidate pool without CED scoring, improves only +1.40pp over SFT s42 versus +4.92pp for CED RSFT, confirming that CED scoring precision drives the majority of the RSFT gain. Increasing $k$ to 3 slightly degrades performance (43.64 Ign-F1), consistent with the intuition that stricter selection yields higher-quality training data. The flat-NLI scoring variant produces comparable Rel-F1 (mean 45.61 vs.\ 45.63 for CED, a difference of 0.02pp). Both CED and flat-NLI improve substantially over the SFT baseline while maintaining or improving Evi-F1, confirming that the RSFT gains are driven by quality-based data selection rather than by the specific contrastive formulation.
43	
44	\paragraph{NLI scoring comparison.} Across all available seeds, CED RSFT achieves mean Rel-F1 of 45.63 (seeds 42, 43, 44, 45: range 45.14--46.21), and flat-NLI RSFT achieves mean Rel-F1 of 45.61 (seeds 42, 43: range 45.35--45.86). The 0.02pp difference suggests comparable performance: CED's contrastive design does not substantially outperform simpler NLI scoring for RSFT data selection. We adopt CED as the default because its contrastive formulation produces per-triple discrimination scores that support interpretable error analysis.
45

113	The 1.7B evidence tax comparison (\S\ref{sec:scaling}) is confounded by differential output quality: the no-evidence model truncates 50.9\% of outputs (501/985 documents) at the \texttt{max\_new\_tokens} limit, versus 31.9\% (314/985) for the evidence model. To control for this, we define a \emph{controlled evaluation subset} that excludes any document where either model produces a truncated or repetitive output. An output is classified as \emph{truncated} if it reaches the generation length limit. An output is classified as \emph{repetitive} if it contains $\geq$3 consecutive identical triples or if the ratio of unique triples to total triples falls below 0.5 (when total $> 5$). The resulting subset contains 442 of 985 development documents (44.9\%). On this subset, the s42 evidence tax is $-$6.2pp (vs.\ $-$8.04pp on the full set), indicating that truncation accounts for approximately 23\% of the gap. The negative direction is preserved, confirming that the 1.7B evidence benefit is genuine and not an artifact of output format differences.

At 4B, duplication is already moderate (31.1\% with evidence), so the regularization benefit diminishes, while the model lacks sufficient capacity to jointly optimize extraction and evidence generation, creating the capacity valley that produces the largest evidence tax (+7.47pp, s42 paired). The truncation asymmetry reverses across scales: at 1.7B the no-evidence model truncates 19pp more often; at 8B the evidence model truncates 9pp more often due to the longer output format.

162	\section{Why RSFT Avoids Decoupling}
163	\label{sec:rsft_theory}
164	
165	The structural difference between selection and optimization explains why RSFT does not exhibit the decoupling observed in gradient-based methods. GRPO and DPO update model parameters through gradients that optimize a reward signal. When two sub-tasks (extraction and evidence) compete for gradient capacity, the optimizer can discover and exploit the trade-off between them, improving one at the expense of the other. RSFT operates differently: it selects complete outputs and trains on them with standard supervised loss. Because the selection is discrete (accept or reject a full response), there is no gradient pathway through which the model can learn to sacrifice extraction for evidence quality. Only outputs where both extraction and evidence are jointly strong survive the CED filter. This property is not specific to RSFT's design but is a structural consequence of discrete selection over complete outputs: any selection-based method that filters on a joint quality criterion will inherit the same coupling guarantee. The implication for practitioners is direct: when optimizing for multiple coupled generation objectives, selection-based methods preserve inter-objective balance that gradient-based methods disrupt.

RSFT CED improves LLaMA to a three-seed mean of 56.54 Ign-F1 (std 0.64pp; s42: 57.14, s43: 56.62, s44: 55.87), a +2.70 point gain over SFT (53.84), consistent with the pattern at the 8B scale (Qwen3-8B: +3.95).

This selective reporting of the most favorable seed introduces some bias. Similarly, at 1.7B the strongest SFT seed inflates the benefit magnitude, though this disclosure issue is inconsistent across scales. The "41× lower standard deviation" claim is technically sound but vulnerable to criticism since it compares across different model scales rather than within them.

Now I'm noticing a terminology issue in the introduction where the phrasing around EDCR values contradicts itself—saying GRPO achieves "mild decoupling" when the EDCR metric actually shows tighter coupling than the SFT baseline, which is the opposite of what the text implies. ) = "Mild"? That's backwards — GRPO bf16 actually has better final EDCR than SFT, so the severity label must be measuring something else entirely, likely the instability during training rather than the endpoint performance. The text confirms this: GRPO bf16 reaches a good checkpoint but takes a variable path to get there, which is why it's marked as "Mild" despite the superior final metrics. This means the table's severity labels and EDCR values are operating on different axes, and that disconnect needs to be flagged as a potential inconsistency in how the results are being presented.

Now I'm reviewing the other updates — the abstract clarification about the three fully evaluated scales with 14B validation is solid, the DPO footnote honestly addresses the earlier evaluation protocol, and the appendix looks comprehensive. Time to compile the full review report.
